title: Seventy-one years: 23 July 2026
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh enters its seventy-second year.
body:
On **23 July 2026**, the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh completed 71 years and entered its seventy-second. The anniversary came days after BMS hosted the BRICS Trade Union Forum in Hyderabad, and just before its all-India working committee met in Ranchi from 26 to 28 July. It is a good moment to look at where the organisation began, how it grew and what it faces now.

## The beginning: Bhopal, 1955

BMS was founded on 23 July 1955, which was also the birth anniversary of Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak. The place was Bhopal and the guiding figure was Dattopant Thengadi. A biographical page maintained by his admirers says the founding meeting had 35 invitees, and that the name was first thought of as Bharatiya Shramik Sangh before being changed to Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh after a suggestion from a delegate from Punjab.

BMS was not formed by splitting an existing union. By its own account, it started with no members, no office and no funds. Before founding it, Thengadi had spent years inside other labour bodies. A page on his life says that from 1949 he studied the labour movement by joining INTUC, became an office bearer of about ten of its unions and joined its national executive in October 1950, and held posts in bank and postal employee organisations until 1955. The idea was to learn how unions worked from inside before starting one with a different outlook.

## The ideas it started with

Several principles were set out early and have stayed constant.

- **Non-political trade unionism.** BMS says it has no tie to any political party. Thengadi's biographers record that he refused to make BMS an affiliate of the Janata Party after the Emergency.
- **Class cooperation, not class conflict.** BMS rejects the Marxist theory of class struggle, though it opposes injustice and exploitation from any source.
- **The motto.** "Nationalise the Labour, Labourise the Industry, Industrialise the Nation", expressed in Hindi as *Rashtrahit, Udyogahit, Shramikahit*: national interest, industry interest and worker interest.
- **Slogan.** *Workers unite the world*, offered in place of "Workers of the world, unite".
- **Maximum production and equitable distribution.** Productivity is treated as a national duty, and fair distribution as the worker's right.
- **Strikes as a last resort.** BMS favours negotiation and arbitration first, and rejects violence.

## Scenes from seventy-one years

- **1955.** A small gathering in Bhopal, with no union affiliated.
- **1967.** The first all-India conference. BMS records 541 affiliated unions and a membership of roughly a quarter of a million, though its own pages give two slightly different figures. Thengadi became General Secretary at that conference.
- **1984 to 1996.** In a Government verification in 1984, BMS was ranked the second-largest central trade union organisation with about 12.1 lakh members. A later verification, whose reference date was 31 December 1989 and whose result was announced in 1996, ranked it the largest, with about 31.2 lakh. BMS says it kept the top position in the next verification in 2002.
- **Today.** BMS claims nearly one crore members, more than 5,000 affiliated unions and presence in all 44 industries that the Labour Ministry classifies for verification. These are BMS's own claims, and readers should note that a verification result is the Government's figure while the present total is BMS's.

In 2026 itself, it held its 21st triennial conference in Odisha from 6 to 8 February, and its elected leadership for 2026-29, with Sunkari Mallesham as National President and Surendra Kumar Pandey as General Secretary, presided over the Ranchi meeting in July.

## What has stayed the same

The motto, the principle of constructive trade unionism, and the working style of karyakartas who give time and sustain the union from their own pockets. The principle that BMS describes as "responsive cooperation" is also unchanged: it judges each policy on its merits, whichever party is in power. In 2025 and 2026 that has meant welcoming the Code on Wages and the Code on Social Security while pressing for amendments to the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code.

BMS also claims to have been the first central union to recognise the self-employed artisan sector, which it calls the Vishwakarma sector, and it marks Vishwakarma Jayanti, in September, as National Labour Day.

## What has changed

The world of work looks different from the one Thengadi entered in 1949.

- **Law.** Since 21 November 2025, four Labour Codes have replaced 29 earlier central laws. For the first time, gig and platform workers have a definition in Indian law.
- **Technology.** Workers now work through apps and platforms, and the new International Labour Organization convention on platform work, adopted in June 2026, is the first global treaty on the subject.
- **Employment form.** Factories have fewer permanent workers, and contract and fixed-term engagement is more common. Women and young people form a larger share of the labour force.
- **Scheme workers.** BMS says more than a crore people, among them Anganwadi, ASHA and mid-day meal workers, work in Government schemes yet are not recognised as workers. It notes that the Anganwadi scheme began in October 1975.

Unions have to organise differently to reach all of these groups.

## The challenge

A movement of seventy years has a history to be proud of and a future to earn. Its leaders have named the "last worker", in Thengadi's tradition of Antyodaya, as the measure. Pressing demands this year include higher pension, wage ceilings for provident fund and insurance coverage, regularisation of contract and scheme workers, and correction of the new Codes. Whether BMS can turn its membership into practical gains for such workers will matter more than any anniversary figure.

## A closing thought

Seventy-one years is a short time in the life of a nation and a long time in the life of a union. What BMS can fairly claim is continuity: the same motto, a steady method of memoranda, meetings and demonstrations, and a growing presence across industries. What it still has to show, as every union must, is that each new generation of workers in factories, offices, fields and on platforms finds in it a voice that is both firm and constructive.
